subject: Design review: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs site-to-site VPN for MedSync on-prem

Hi Lauren —

Thanks — confirming the objectives up front:
- Yes, MedSync requires private-only API access for PHI flows (no public endpoints).
- We have two AWS accounts (prod-apps and prod-data) and an on-prem datacenter with a Palo Alto HA pair.
- Bandwidth profile: steady 200–400 Mbps with spikes up to 800 Mbps during nightly batch windows.
- CIDR ranges: on-prem 10.0.0.0/16, prod-apps 10.1.0.0/16, prod-data 10.2.0.0/16 (no overlaps).

Firewall team contact: Mike Chen <mike.chen@acmeinfra.com> (he manages the datacenter network).

We'd like your recommendation on the minimal blast-radius design and whether we need an intermediary transit VPC or an endpoint approach. Also any notes on monitoring, failover, and how Redwood handles observability of private traffic would be helpful.

Best,

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>
To: Priya Natarajan <pri...@medsync.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 06 Oct 2026 08:27:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Design review: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs VPN for MedSync private deployment

Hi Priya, Mike, Anil —

Thanks for the details — this helps. Below is our concise assessment tailored to your constraints (private-only, multiple accounts, non-overlapping CIDRs, 200–800 Mbps burst):

1) VPC Peering- Pros:
  • Low latency, direct L3 connectivity between VPCs.
  • Simple routing; no proxying.
  • Cost: no per-endpoint data processing charges — just inter-AZ/data transfer.

  Cons / constraints:
  • No transitive peering — you'll need either point-to-point peering between each pair or a transit (AWS Transit Gateway). With prod-apps + prod-data + Redwood-managed VPCs, peering quickly scales poorly.
  • Cross-account peering is supported but adds management complexity and permissions.
  • Not ideal if you want to isolate Redwood's control plane from customer VPCs — peering gives broad network visibility (routing tables).

When to pick: small number of VPCs, trust model where MedSync is comfortable adding route entries into customer VPCs, and you want minimal latency/cost overhead.

2) AWS PrivateLink (VPC Endpoints)- Pros:
  • Service endpoints expose only the service interface (L4/L7) — much smaller attack surface and minimal routing changes on the customer side.
  • Works cross-account without exposing entire VPC routing tables.
  • No CIDR planning between client and service VPCs; easier both for security and ops.
  • Good for multi-account SaaS patterns — Redwood keeps its service in our VPC and you connect via ENIs in your VPC.

  Cons / constraints:
  • Additional per-GB endpoint charges and NLB costs (if we front with NLB). For heavy egress (hundreds of MBps sustained), cost matters.
  • Max throughput per endpoint vs needed burst — you can scale via multiple endpoints and NLBs, but that's operational overhead.
  • Some protocols and custom TCP behaviors can need tuning.

When to pick: security-first setups where minimal blast radius and limited network visibility are required; preferred for customer-facing private APIs and multi-account SaaS.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPSec)- Pros:
  • Straightforward for connecting on-prem to cloud; you already have a Palo Alto HA pair.
  • Can be resilient with dual tunnels to two AZs / TGW attachments.
  • Lower setup complexity if the on-prem team prefers a single endpoint and you don't want to manage cross-account cloud routing.

  Cons / constraints:
  • Latency higher and jitter more than private cloud connectivity; depends on ISP.
  • Throughput for VPNs is often limited by device capacity and can be more expensive to scale for 800 Mbps bursts.
  • Additional management for pre-shared keys, rotations, and lifecycle of tunnel endpoints.

When to pick: when strict on-prem connectivity is required (direct datacenter-only clients) or as a fallback/high-availability complement to PrivateLink.

Recommendation for MedSync (based on objectives):
  • Primary: AWS PrivateLink for Redwood service endpoints into your prod-data and prod-apps accounts. This minimizes blast radius, avoids broad routing changes, and satisfies PHI isolation requirements.
  • Secondary / HA: Maintain a site-to-site VPN from on-prem to a transit VPC or directly to prod-data for batch window traffic and as an alternate path in case of PrivateLink region issues.
  • Transit considerations: If MedSync plans to scale to many VPCs, add an AWS Transit Gateway in your account to centralize VPN attachments and manage routing cleanly. Redwood can peer our management VPC to a controlled endpoint (or expose PrivateLink into each target VPC) per your security preference.

Operational notes we will provide if you select PrivateLink:
  • Endpoint capacity planning guidance (we'll size NLB + ENI counts; see attached Excel).
  • Runbook for failover between PrivateLink and VPN (sample BGP/static routes for quick cutover).
  • Monitoring: flow logs + VPC endpoint CloudWatch metrics + application-layer tracing we surface in Redwood Console.
  • Compliance evidence: SOC2 artifacts and network diagrams (attached).

Open questions for your network team:
  1) Do you want Redwood-managed endpoints (we create the endpoint service and manage the NLB) or customer-managed endpoints (we give you the service name and you create interface endpoints)?
  2) For the batch windows (up to 800 Mbps), do you prefer traffic to flow over PrivateLink (recommended) or to burst to the site-to-site VPN?
  3) Do you already have a Transit Gateway or should we plan for per-VPC endpoints in the short term?

I've attached a short tradeoffs PDF and a sizing spreadsheet for PrivateLink. Happy to walk through on a call — proposed time Monday 10/6 10:30 PT or Tuesday 10/7 11:00 PT.

Thanks,
Karthik

Date: Thu, 07 Oct 2026 15:48:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Design review: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs VPN for MedSync private deployment

Karthik / Lauren —

Thanks, this is very clear and helpful. After internal discussion with the security and operations teams (Mike looped in), we agreed on the following:

Decision summary:
- Primary connectivity: AWS PrivateLink (customer-managed interface endpoints) into both prod-apps and prod-data. We want the tighter isolation and to avoid additional routing exposure.
- HA / backup: Site-to-site VPN from on-prem to our Transit Gateway (we will provision TGW) for batch-window fallback and DR.
- No VPC peering at this time. If we expand to many additional VPCs later, we'll revisit Transit Gateway.

On the implementation items: Mike will share our firewall IP allowlist and the Palo Alto config snippets. He flagged that for 800 Mbps sustained bursts we'll need two parallel VPN tunnels if we ever route batch over VPN — agree that PrivateLink should be primary for day-to-day traffic.

Next steps:
- Mike (on-prem) to send firewall rules + contact window by EOD 10/08.
- MedSync to create the interface endpoints and share endpoint IDs; Redwood will provide the service name and NLB details.
- Redwood (Karthik) to provide endpoint capacity guidance and the cutover runbook by 10/12.
- Exchange SOC2 & network diagrams in shared Drive (link above).

Appreciate the clear tradeoffs. We'll target a joint runbook review the week of 10/18.

Best,
Priya
Priya Natarajan
Head of Engineering, MedSync
